candidates.claim: The speculation relies on high similarity between consecutive attention-layer inputs due to outliers and LayerNorm; if a model lacks this property, the previous-layer rehearsal is a poor predictor.
candidates.mechanism: Paper uses Layer i-1 attention input to speculate Layer i -> premise: consecutive attention inputs are highly similar -> if similarity is low, the partial rehearsal ranks tokens differently from the actual next-layer attention.
candidates.conditions: Consecutive attention inputs must be highly similar and outlier channels must be present.
candidates.consequence: Wrong KV entries may be prefetched, causing accuracy loss.
candidates.defeaters: The limitation is irrelevant if the target model empirically preserves high consecutive-layer input similarity.

candidates.claim: The method assumes attention is sparse enough that dropping low-score tokens preserves accuracy; tasks with diffuse attention may violate this assumption.
candidates.mechanism: Paper says skipping less critical tokens does not significantly degrade accuracy if selection is appropriate -> premise: a few tokens dominate attention -> if attention is diffuse, many tokens are jointly important and selection becomes lossy.
candidates.conditions: Attention weights must be concentrated on a small subset of tokens.
candidates.consequence: Accuracy may drop on tasks requiring broad or diffuse attention.
candidates.defeaters: The limitation is irrelevant if the target workload has strongly sparse attention.

quotes.quote: skipping attention computation for some less critical tokens does not significantly degrade the model accuracy, provided the token selection is appropriate.

evidence.support_description: skipping attention computation for some less critical tokens does not significantly degrade the model accuracy, provided the token selection is appropriate.

candidates.claim: The method requires offline access to model weights and a representative sample input to compute SVD-based skewing; black-box or dynamically changing models cannot use it directly.
candidates.mechanism: Paper runs a forward pass once with a sample input and modifies weight matrices -> premise: full model weights are accessible and stable -> API-only models or models with runtime weight changes cannot be skewed in this way.
candidates.conditions: Full model weights must be accessible and stable enough for one-time offline modification.
candidates.consequence: InfiniGen cannot be applied to proprietary API models or models whose weights change at runtime.
candidates.defeaters: The limitation is irrelevant if the deployment can modify weights or if skewing is omitted with acceptable accuracy.

candidates.claim: The provided implementation assumes standard multi-head attention with equal Q, K, and V head counts; it reshapes K with n_head and head_dim derived from the hidden size.
candidates.mechanism: Code computes head_dim = h // n_head and reshapes k to (b, s, n_head, head_dim) -> premise: K must have the same number of heads as Q -> grouped-query or multi-query attention with fewer KV heads cannot be represented without code changes.
candidates.conditions: The model must use standard MHA or an adapted implementation where K/V head counts match Q.
candidates.consequence: The method cannot be applied directly to GQA/MQA models or would mis-shape tensors.
candidates.defeaters: The limitation is irrelevant if the target model uses standard MHA or the code is adapted for GQA/MQA.

candidates.claim: Speculation uses only the previous-layer attention input and partial Q/K of the next layer, ignoring the current layer's actual Q/K/V, so it can misrank tokens when the next layer's attention differs.
candidates.mechanism: Paper uses Layer i-1 input and partial Layer i Q/K -> premise: the next layer is predictable from the previous layer -> if actual current Q/K/V select different tokens, the prefetched set misses important KV entries.
candidates.conditions: The next-layer attention pattern must be well predicted by the previous-layer rehearsal.
candidates.consequence: Important KV entries may be omitted, reducing accuracy.
candidates.defeaters: The limitation is irrelevant if the prediction is accurate for the target model and workload.

candidates.claim: The alpha threshold uses an absolute score difference from the maximum, so its effect depends on score scale and distribution; a fixed alpha can select too few or too many tokens.
candidates.mechanism: Paper selects scores greater than max minus alpha -> softmax converts the score difference into a ratio -> if score scale varies across layers or models, the same alpha changes the selected set size and accuracy.
candidates.conditions: The score scale must be stable enough for a fixed alpha to be meaningful.
candidates.consequence: The method may overfetch or underfetch KV entries, trading accuracy for bandwidth poorly.
candidates.defeaters: The limitation is irrelevant if alpha is calibrated per layer/model or score scales are stable.

candidates.claim: The paper enforces the same number of prefetched tokens across heads by averaging, and the code averages across all heads and batch elements, so heterogeneous attention sparsity is flattened.
candidates.mechanism: Paper says each head fetches the same number of tokens -> code computes mean = torch.mean(torch.sum(count, dim=-1)).item() -> a head or request needing many tokens is underfetched while another needing few is overfetched.
candidates.conditions: Heads or batch requests must have different attention sparsity for the averaging to hurt.
candidates.consequence: Accuracy loss or wasted PCIe bandwidth.
candidates.defeaters: The limitation is irrelevant if sparsity is homogeneous or the max_num_kv cap dominates.

candidates.consequence: Accuracy may drop in layers with broad attention.
candidates.defeaters: The limitation is irrelevant if important sets always remain below the cap.

candidates.claim: Under a CPU memory limit, the counter-based eviction can permanently remove KV entries that are temporarily unimportant but later become important.
candidates.mechanism: Paper selects a victim with the smallest count -> counters increment on prefetch and halve on saturation -> a token not recently prefetched can be evicted even if future attention would need it.
candidates.conditions: The CPU memory limit must be reached and attention importance must change over iterations.
candidates.consequence: Permanent context loss and accuracy drop under memory pressure.
candidates.defeaters: The limitation is irrelevant if no memory limit is used or the counter policy preserves all future-important tokens.

candidates.consequence: Token selection and model accuracy may degrade due to miscalibrated attention scores.
candidates.defeaters: The limitation is irrelevant if scaling is applied elsewhere or the weights are pre-scaled.
